Everyone should have a patch of land that they care for. Potted plants and gardens are great, but much of the wildlands have been severely disturbed with little remediation. Being a landless fellow myself, I have adopted several places in the countryside.

Specifically, it is good to know which plants are local and which are invasive, meaning they will form a monoculture without intervention. Along the west coast of the US this includes English ivies and hollys, Argentinian pampas and jubata grasses, Scotch broom, bull thistles and Himalayan blackberries.

The best use of these plants is to mulch them into a new soil layer for the area. This quickly replenishes soil which is often thin and impacted, while providing safe places for insects which will in turn boost the food chain of the area. More bugs leads to more spiders, bats, lizards and small birds, which will in turn lure predator birds, who will regulate the crow and starling population, etc. From small actions a larger result can become evident, if you are persistent. This is why adopting a small area is best.

This approach is best done slowly, to allow the biome time to adjust. For example, insects will colonize trash heaps as readily as they would a pile of leaf litter, and mice and quail will take shelter in blackberry bushes if they have no other options. In order to connect with the land, any time spent on work should be matched by an equal time of observation. Nature is complex, and many important details can be missed if one is hasty or preoccupied.

I could go on, but the point is having a relationship with the Earth is just as important as having relationships with your community. Pic is of one of my wild places, where I go occasionally to cut weeds and hunt rabbits.

English Ivy is indeed a tough one, even the merest contact with the ground can cause new roots to form. Most of the time I don't have the ability to remove the material from the area so I've learned a few tricks, but it still requires more attention than other weeds.

The main thing to consider is that each piece of vine can regrow into a new plant, so taking care not to break the vines any more than necessary helps quite a lot. Instead, bend and kink the vines without breaking it off, so that the plant is distressed and exposed to pathogens. In small amounts, the ivy can be hung to dry on tree branches. For the larger patches I bundled the ivy into a thick clump, and turned the pile every few days. After a month (in dry weather) the pile is dry enough to leave be. Spiders especially love mounds of dead ivy.
